title: Chapter 9: Monopolistic Competition, Oligopoly, and Game Theory

questions.title: Defining Traits of Monopolistic Competition
questions.prompt_template: Which combination of market characteristics defines monopolistic competition?

hints.text: Think of monopolistic competition as a hybrid of perfect competition and monopoly.
Ask how many sellers participate, whether products are identical or differentiated, and whether long-run entry is free or blocked.

options_template.text: Many competing sellers, differentiated products, and free entry and exit in the long run.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Monopolistic competition combines many sellers and free long-run entry/exit (like perfect competition) with differentiated products (creating modest price-making power).

options_template.text: Many competing sellers, identical standardized products, and free entry and exit in the long run.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Perfect Competition Confusion): Identical standardized products with many sellers and free entry define perfect competition, not monopolistic competition.

options_template.text: A handful of large sellers, differentiated products, and high barriers to entry.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Oligopoly Confusion): A small number of dominant sellers protected by significant barriers to entry characterizes an oligopoly, not monopolistic competition.

options_template.text: A single dominant seller, a unique product with no close substitutes, and blocked entry.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Pure Monopoly Confusion): A single seller with blocked entry and no close substitutes defines a pure monopoly.

questions.title: Why a Monopolistically Competitive Firm Faces Downward-Sloping Demand
questions.prompt_template: Why does an individual neighborhood coffee shop under monopolistic competition face a downward-sloping demand curve rather than a horizontal demand curve?

hints.text: Compare how customers respond to a slight price hike when goods are unique versus identical.
Product differentiation builds brand loyalty so raising price loses some customers, not all of them.

options_template.text: Legal zoning rules prevent any new coffee shop from opening in the same city.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Entry-Barrier Confusion): Monopolistic competition features free long-run entry and exit; downward-sloping demand stems from differentiation, not blocked entry.

options_template.text: Product differentiation gives the shop limited brand loyalty, so raising price loses some customers without driving sales immediately to zero.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because each café offers a distinct roast, ambiance, or location, rival shops are imperfect substitutes, giving the firm modest price-setting power and a downward-sloping demand curve.

options_template.text: Each coffee shop is so large that it supplies the entire national market for coffee.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Market-Size Fallacy): Monopolistically competitive markets contain many small sellers, none of which supplies the entire market.

options_template.text: The shop's marginal cost curve slopes upward at all output levels.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Demand Conflation): The shape of a firm's cost curves reflects production technology and input prices, not the slope of its consumer demand curve.

questions.title: Interpreting Zero Long-Run Economic Profit
questions.prompt_template: In long-run monopolistic competition, firms earn zero economic profit (P = ATC). What does zero economic profit imply for the business owner's accounting profit?

hints.text: Distinguish explicit accounting expenses from implicit opportunity costs.
Recall that ATC in economics includes both explicit costs and the owner's normal profit (opportunity cost of time and capital).

options_template.text: The owner earns zero accounting profit and cannot pay rent, wages, or suppliers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Accounting-Economic Conflation): Zero economic profit still covers all explicit bills (rent, wages, supplies) plus a competitive return to the owner.

options_template.text: The owner incurs an accounting loss each year and must borrow to stay open.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Loss Misinterpretation): When P = ATC, total revenue equals total economic cost, so the firm breaks even economically and earns positive accounting profit.

options_template.text: The owner earns a positive normal (accounting) profit that covers all explicit bills plus the full opportunity cost of the owner's time and invested capital.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Zero economic profit means the owner earns exactly a normal profit—covering explicit operating costs and earning as much as their time and capital would earn in their next-best alternative.

options_template.text: The owner earns monopoly-level economic returns indefinitely because of brand loyalty.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Barrier-Free Persistence Fallacy): Free entry erodes above-normal economic profits in the long run even when products are differentiated.

questions.title: Excess Capacity and Markup in Long-Run Monopolistic Competition
questions.prompt_template: Which pair of permanent structural features characterizes a monopolistically competitive firm in long-run equilibrium?

hints.text: Compare the firm's long-run price P_LR against MC_LR, and compare its output q_LR against efficient scale q_eff.
Check both allocative efficiency (P vs. MC) and productive efficiency (q_LR vs. minimum ATC).

options_template.text: Price equals marginal cost (P = MC) and output occurs at minimum average total cost (q_LR = q_eff).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Perfect Competition Attribution): P = MC and production at minimum ATC describe long-run perfect competition, not monopolistic competition.

options_template.text: Price equals marginal cost (P = MC) while the firm operates strictly above minimum average total cost.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Markup Omission): Because demand slopes downward, MR lies below P, so setting MR = MC guarantees a markup (P > MC).

options_template.text: Price exceeds average total cost (P > ATC) while output exceeds efficient scale (q_LR > q_eff).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Long-Run Profit Error): Free entry eliminates long-run profit so P = ATC, and tangency to downward-sloping ATC keeps q_LR strictly below q_eff.

options_template.text: A positive markup over marginal cost (P > MC) and excess capacity (q_LR < q_eff).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Long-run tangency to the left of minimum ATC generates both allocative inefficiency (markup P > MC) and productive inefficiency (excess capacity q_LR < q_eff).

questions.title: Role of Non-Price Competition in Monopolistic Competition
questions.prompt_template: Why do monopolistically competitive firms such as hair salons, boutiques, and cafés invest heavily in branding, store ambiance, and targeted advertising?

hints.text: Consider how firms attract loyal customers without starting destructive price cuts.
Non-price competition reinforces how consumers perceive a firm's product relative to nearby rivals.

options_template.text: To strengthen product differentiation and customer brand loyalty so they can retain some price-setting power.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Non-price competition (branding, ambiance, convenience, and advertising) accentuates product differentiation and makes rivals less close substitutes.

options_template.text: To eliminate product differences so that consumers view all firms' offerings as identical commodities.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Standardization Inversion): Making products identical would destroy brand loyalty and push the firm toward price-taking behavior.

options_template.text: To raise legal barriers that permanently forbid any rival from entering the neighborhood.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Legal-Barrier Confusion): Advertising and ambiance cannot legally block entry in monopolistically competitive markets.

options_template.text: To guarantee that marginal revenue equals price at every quantity sold.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (MR-Price Identity Error): Only a price-taking perfectly competitive firm with horizontal demand has MR = P; differentiation keeps MR below P.

questions.title: Defining Features of an Oligopoly
questions.prompt_template: Which market description best represents an oligopoly such as commercial aircraft manufacturing or national wireless telecom carriers?

hints.text: Focus on the number of dominant firms and why new competitors cannot easily enter.
Recall the role of economies of scale, spectrum licenses, patents, and network effects.

options_template.text: Hundreds of independent regional firms with zero entry costs and identical service plans.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Perfect Competition Description): Many small firms with zero barriers and identical products define perfect competition.

options_template.text: A handful of large firms protected by significant barriers to entry whose decisions directly affect one another.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Oligopolies consist of a few dominant sellers insulated by high entry barriers (economies of scale, spectrum licenses, patents, or network effects) who exhibit strategic interdependence.

options_template.text: Dozens of small neighborhood sellers offering differentiated styles with free long-run entry.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Monopolistic Competition Confusion): Many small sellers with free entry and product differentiation define monopolistic competition.

options_template.text: A single government-franchised utility serving all customers with no rivals.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Pure Monopoly Confusion): A single seller with no rivals is a pure monopoly, not an oligopoly.

questions.title: Meaning of Strategic Interdependence
questions.prompt_template: What do economists mean by strategic interdependence in an oligopoly?

hints.text: Think about how a small number of rivals react when one firm changes its price or launches a new product.
Ask whether an oligopolist can maximize profit by ignoring its competitors' likely responses.

options_template.text: Firms share the same input suppliers, so every firm has identical average total cost.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Sharing Confusion): Common input suppliers affect cost curves across any market structure; strategic interdependence concerns rival firms' mutual reactions in the output market.

options_template.text: Every firm must sign a legally binding profit-sharing contract before entering the market.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Mandatory Collusion Fallacy): Strategic interdependence exists even when firms compete non-cooperatively without any contract.

options_template.text: Each firm's pricing, output, or advertising decision directly affects rivals' sales and profits and triggers counter-moves.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because only a few large firms share the market, each firm must anticipate how rivals will react before choosing its own price, output, or marketing strategy.

options_template.text: Consumers depend entirely on one firm because no substitutes exist.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Monopoly Conflation): Having no substitutes describes pure monopoly, where there are no direct rivals to interact with strategically.

questions.title: Why Cartels Face Inherent Internal Instability
questions.prompt_template: Once an oligopoly cartel restricts industry output to hold the market price well above marginal cost (P > MC), why is the cartel inherently unstable?

hints.text: Compare the collective goal of the cartel with the unilateral incentive of one individual member.
What happens to an individual member's profit if it secretly sells extra units slightly below the cartel price while rivals restrict output?

options_template.text: Cartel members always earn negative economic profits whenever industry output is restricted.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cartel Profit Inversion): Restricting output toward the monopoly level raises joint industry profits; instability comes from the temptation to earn even more by cheating.

options_template.text: Restricting output forces every member's marginal cost to rise above the cartel price.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Direction Inversion): Under standard rising or constant marginal cost, lowering output does not push MC above the elevated cartel price.

options_template.text: Market demand automatically becomes perfectly elastic whenever firms coordinate output.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Elasticity Fallacy): Collusion does not alter underlying consumer preferences or make market demand horizontal.

options_template.text: Because P > MC, each individual member can raise its own profit by secretly undercutting price or exceeding its quota to steal rivals' customers.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Since each extra unit sold near the cartel price adds (P - MC) > 0 to an individual cheater's profit, every member faces a strong temptation to defect, eventually eroding the cartel.

questions.title: Comparing the Four-Firm Concentration Ratio and the HHI
questions.prompt_template: How does the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) differ from the Four-Firm Concentration Ratio (CR4) in measuring industry concentration?

hints.text: Look at the mathematical formula HHI = s_1^2 + s_2^2 + ... + s_N^2 versus CR4 = s_1 + s_2 + s_3 + s_4.
Notice which measure includes all firms and places greater weight on large market shares.

options_template.text: HHI sums the squared percentage market shares of all firms (ranging up to 10,000 for a pure monopoly), giving greater weight to larger firms and capturing share distribution.
options_template.feedback: Correct. By squaring every firm's percentage market share, HHI reflects both total market structure and inequality among leading firms, whereas CR4 simply sums the top four shares.

options_template.text: CR4 squares the top four firms' shares and reaches a maximum of 10,000, whereas HHI sums shares without squaring them.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Formula Swap): It is HHI that squares market shares (reaching 10,000 for a 100% monopoly), while CR4 simply adds the four largest percentage shares (max 100%).

options_template.text: HHI measures a firm's price-cost markup (P - MC), whereas CR4 measures excess capacity.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Metric Conflation): Both CR4 and HHI measure market-share concentration, not price-cost markups or excess capacity.

options_template.text: CR4 includes every firm in the industry, whereas HHI counts only the single largest firm.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Scope Inversion): CR4 looks only at the top four firms, while HHI sums squared shares across all N firms in the market.

questions.title: Three Essential Building Blocks of a Strategic Game
questions.prompt_template: In microeconomic game theory, which three essential components define any strategic game?

hints.text: Think about what information you must put into a payoff matrix before you can analyze it.
You need to know who is deciding, what actions they can pick, and what outcomes result.

options_template.text: Fixed costs, variable costs, and efficient scale.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Structure Confusion): Cost categories describe firm production technology rather than the formal structure of a strategic game.

options_template.text: The players, the strategies available to each player, and the payoffs resulting from every combination of choices.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Every strategic game is fully specified by its players, each player's strategy set, and the payoffs assigned to every profile of strategy choices.

options_template.text: The four-firm concentration ratio, the HHI, and antitrust merger thresholds.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Concentration-Index Confusion): CR4 and HHI measure industry structure, not the formal elements of a game.

options_template.text: Binding cartel contracts, government price floors, and consumer subsidies.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Institutional Conflation): Non-cooperative game theory explicitly analyzes rational strategic choices without binding cartel contracts.

questions.title: Definition of a Strictly Dominant Strategy
questions.prompt_template: In a simultaneous strategic game, when does a firm have a strictly dominant strategy?

hints.text: Ask whether the firm's optimal action depends on guessing what its rival will do.
Check if one specific choice outperforms all alternatives across every possible rival move.

options_template.text: When the strategy maximizes the combined profits of all firms in the industry.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Joint-Profit Confusion): A dominant strategy maximizes an individual player's own payoff regardless of rivals' actions; in a Prisoner's Dilemma, it actually lowers joint profits.

options_template.text: When the strategy yields a higher payoff only if the rival agrees to cooperate.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Conditional Best-Response Error): A strategy that is optimal only against one specific rival action is a conditional best response, not a dominant strategy.

options_template.text: When the strategy yields a strictly higher payoff for that firm no matter what strategy its rival chooses.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A strictly dominant strategy beats every alternative action under every possible strategy the rival might select, so a rational player always plays it.

options_template.text: When the firm holds more than 50% of total market sales.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Market-Share Wordplay): 'Dominant strategy' is a game-theoretic optimality property of an action, not a measure of market share.

questions.title: Definition of a Nash Equilibrium
questions.prompt_template: Which condition defines a Nash equilibrium in a strategic game?

hints.text: Ask whether any single player has an incentive to switch strategies on their own.
In a Nash equilibrium, every player's chosen strategy is a best response to the strategies chosen by all other players.

options_template.text: Players sign an enforceable legal agreement that prevents anyone from lowering prices.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Binding-Contract Confusion): Nash equilibrium predicts self-enforcing outcomes without binding contracts.

options_template.text: All players earn the highest possible combined profit available anywhere in the payoff matrix.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Pareto-Optimality Conflation): A Nash equilibrium need not maximize joint payoffs—as demonstrated by the low-profit Nash equilibrium in a Prisoner's Dilemma.

options_template.text: Every player must possess a strictly dominant strategy.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Dominance-Requirement Fallacy): Dominant-strategy equilibria are always Nash equilibria, but a Nash equilibrium can exist even when one or more players lack a dominant strategy.

options_template.text: Every player is choosing their best response given what the other players are doing, so no player can improve their payoff by unilaterally changing strategy.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A Nash equilibrium is a self-enforcing profile of mutual best responses where no player can gain by deviating unilaterally.

questions.title: Core Paradox of the Prisoner's Dilemma
questions.prompt_template: What is the central economic paradox illustrated by a one-shot Prisoner's Dilemma between two competing firms?

hints.text: Compare what happens when both firms pursue individual self-interest versus when both cooperate.
Notice how dominant strategies interact with joint profitability.

options_template.text: Each firm's individually rational dominant strategy to defect leads both firms into a Nash equilibrium with lower profits than if both had cooperated.
options_template.feedback: Correct. In a Prisoner's Dilemma, individual rationality drives each player to defect, trapping both in an outcome strictly worse for them than mutual cooperation.

options_template.text: Firms fail to reach any Nash equilibrium because neither firm can predict the other's move.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (No-Equilibrium Error): A Prisoner's Dilemma has a clear, unique Nash equilibrium—namely mutual defection.

options_template.text: Consumers always suffer higher prices whenever rival firms fail to cooperate.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Welfare Inversion): When competing firms fail to sustain high-price collusion in a pricing Prisoner's Dilemma, consumers actually benefit from lower prices and higher surplus.

options_template.text: Cooperation is each firm's strictly dominant strategy, yet firms mistakenly choose defection due to irrationality.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Irrationality Misattribution): Defection—not cooperation—is each firm's strictly dominant strategy; the low-profit outcome results from rational self-interest, not irrationality.

questions.title: Curve Shift Following Short-Run Positive Economic Profits
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a boutique fitness studio in a monopolistically competitive neighborhood currently operates where MR = MC and charges a price strictly above its ATC curve (P > ATC). How does the firm's diagram adjust in the long run?

hints.text: Ask whether positive economic profits attract new firms into the neighborhood or push existing firms out.
When new competitors draw away customers, which direction does each incumbent firm's demand curve shift?

options_template.text: New studios enter the market, shifting each incumbent firm's demand (D) curve rightward (outward) until P = MC.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Entry Shift Inversion): Entry splits market customers among more rivals, shifting each incumbent's individual demand curve leftward, not rightward.

options_template.text: New studios enter the market, shifting each incumbent firm's demand (D) and MR curves leftward (inward) until D is tangent to ATC.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Positive economic profits attract entry under free entry/exit, reducing each incumbent's market share and shifting its D and MR curves inward until P = ATC (zero economic profit).

options_template.text: Incumbent studios expand output along their existing demand curve until price falls to minimum ATC.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Movement vs. Shift Error): Long-run entry changes the number of rivals, which shifts each firm's demand curve inward rather than causing a movement along a fixed demand curve.

options_template.text: The firm's ATC curve shifts downward until minimum ATC equals the original short-run price.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Shift Confusion): Entry of rivals affects demand for an incumbent's product rather than lowering the incumbent's production cost curve.

questions.title: Curve Shift Following Short-Run Economic Losses
questions.prompt_template: In a monopolistically competitive restaurant market, typical firms are currently maximizing profit (minimizing loss) at MR = MC where price lies strictly below ATC (P < ATC). How does the diagram for a surviving restaurant adjust in the long run?

hints.text: Ask what happens to the number of restaurants in the neighborhood when owners earn below-normal returns.
As some restaurants close, what happens to the customer base of each remaining restaurant?

options_template.text: Rival restaurants exit, shifting each remaining restaurant's demand (D) and MR curves leftward until P = MC.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Exit Shift Inversion): When rivals exit, their former customers flow to surviving restaurants, shifting remaining firms' demand curves rightward, not leftward.

options_template.text: No exit occurs because product differentiation guarantees every restaurant stays open permanently.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Free-Exit Omission): Monopolistic competition features free exit; firms earning sustained economic losses eventually leave the industry.

options_template.text: Rival restaurants exit, shifting each remaining restaurant's demand (D) and MR curves rightward (outward) until D becomes tangent to ATC.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Short-run losses trigger exit; as rivals leave, surviving firms gain customers, shifting their D and MR curves outward until zero economic profit (P = ATC) is restored.

options_template.text: Remaining restaurants' demand curves flatten into a horizontal line at minimum ATC.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Differentiation Loss Error): Exit reduces the number of rivals without making remaining restaurants identical, so their demand curves remain downward-sloping.

questions.title: Why Long-Run Tangency Occurs Strictly Left of Minimum ATC
questions.prompt_template: In the long-run equilibrium diagram for monopolistic competition, why must the tangency point between the firm's demand curve (D) and its U-shaped ATC curve lie strictly to the left of the minimum point of ATC?

hints.text: Compare the slope of two tangent curves at their exact point of tangency.
What is the sign of the slope of D, and where on a U-shaped ATC curve does ATC have that same sign of slope?

options_template.text: Because the demand curve is upward-sloping, forcing tangency onto the rising portion of ATC.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand Slope Error): Firm demand curves slope downward, not upward, so tangency cannot occur on the upward-sloping branch of ATC.

options_template.text: Because ATC is horizontal everywhere to the left of efficient scale.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (ATC Shape Error): A U-shaped ATC curve slopes downward to the left of its minimum and is horizontal (zero slope) only at the single minimum point q_eff.

options_template.text: Because marginal cost lies above ATC at all output levels below efficient scale.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (MC-ATC Relationship Inversion): To the left of minimum ATC, ATC is falling, which requires MC < ATC, not MC > ATC.

options_template.text: Because tangency requires equal slopes, and since D slopes downward, D can only be tangent to ATC on the downward-sloping portion of ATC to the left of its minimum.
options_template.feedback: Correct. At tangency, the slope of D equals the slope of ATC. Because D slopes downward (negative slope), ATC must also be sloping downward at q_LR, which lies strictly to the left of minimum ATC.

questions.topic: Reading the Long-Run Monopolistic Competition Diagram
questions.title: Locating Equilibrium Price, Quantity, and Markup on the Graph
questions.prompt_template: On the standard long-run monopolistic competition graph (showing D, MR, MC, and ATC), how do you locate the firm's equilibrium output q_LR, price P_LR, and per-unit markup over marginal cost?

hints.text: Start with the profit-maximizing rule MR = MC to find quantity on the horizontal axis.
Then trace vertically at q_LR to find the price consumers pay on D and the marginal cost on MC.

options_template.text: Find q_LR where MR intersects MC; trace up to D (where D is tangent to ATC) to read P_LR; the vertical gap between P_LR and MC_LR at q_LR is the markup.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Profit maximization sets MR = MC to determine q_LR, price P_LR = ATC is read vertically on D, and the vertical segment (P_LR - MC_LR) directly measures the markup.

options_template.text: Find q_LR at the minimum point of ATC; then read P_LR from the MR curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Efficient-Scale Fallacy): Monopolistically competitive firms produce strictly below minimum ATC, and price is always read on the demand curve D, never on MR.

options_template.text: Find q_LR where D intersects MC; then read P_LR from the ATC curve and markup as ATC minus D.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Competitive Rule Error): A firm with a downward-sloping demand curve maximizes profit at MR = MC, not P = MC.

options_template.text: Find q_LR where MR intersects the horizontal axis; then read P_LR where MC intersects ATC.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Revenue-Maximization Error): MR = 0 maximizes total revenue rather than profit (unless MC = 0), and MC = ATC identifies q_eff, not P_LR.

questions.title: Identifying Excess Capacity on the Long-Run Graph
questions.prompt_template: On the long-run equilibrium diagram of a monopolistically competitive firm, which geometric distance represents excess capacity?

hints.text: Ask whether excess capacity is measured in dollars (vertical axis) or units of output (horizontal axis).
Locate both q_LR (where MR = MC) and q_eff (where MC crosses minimum ATC).

options_template.text: The vertical distance between P_LR on the demand curve and MC_LR at output q_LR.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Axis Confusion — Markup vs. Excess Capacity): The vertical gap (P_LR - MC_LR) measures the dollar markup over marginal cost, not excess capacity.

options_template.text: The horizontal distance between the long-run profit-maximizing output q_LR and the efficient-scale output q_eff at minimum ATC.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Excess capacity equals (q_eff - q_LR)—the horizontal output shortfall between where the firm actually produces and the output that minimizes ATC.

options_template.text: The vertical distance between P_LR and the minimum point of ATC.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Premium Confusion): The vertical difference (P_LR - min ATC) measures the higher average cost per unit, whereas excess capacity is the horizontal output gap (q_eff - q_LR).

options_template.text: The horizontal distance between the vertical axis (q = 0) and the output where MR = 0.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Output-Intercept Confusion): The distance from 0 to where MR = 0 is the revenue-maximizing quantity, unrelated to efficient scale or excess capacity.

questions.topic: Comparing Long-Run Diagrams: Perfect vs. Monopolistic Competition
questions.title: Graphical Contrast Between Perfect and Monopolistic Competition
questions.prompt_template: Comparing long-run equilibrium diagrams for a perfectly competitive firm and a monopolistically competitive firm, which graphical statement is accurate?

hints.text: Compare the tangency of D to ATC in both models.
In both models zero economic profit holds (P = ATC), but the slope of D differs.

options_template.text: Both firms produce at minimum ATC, but only the monopolistically competitive firm charges a markup above MC.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Tangency Geometry Violation): If a firm produced at minimum ATC with P = ATC, then since MC = ATC at minimum ATC, it would have P = MC and zero markup.

options_template.text: The perfectly competitive firm earns zero economic profit (P = ATC), whereas the monopolistically competitive firm preserves positive profit (P > ATC) in the long run.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Long-Run Profit Fallacy): Free entry drives long-run economic profit to zero (P = ATC) in both perfect competition and monopolistic competition.

options_template.text: Both firms produce where P = ATC, but the perfectly competitive firm's horizontal D is tangent at minimum ATC (P = MC), while the monopolistically competitive firm's downward-sloping D is tangent left of minimum ATC (P > MC).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Free entry drives P = ATC in both markets, yet horizontal demand pins perfect competition to minimum ATC and P = MC, whereas downward-sloping demand creates excess capacity and P > MC under monopolistic competition.

options_template.text: The perfectly competitive firm operates with excess capacity because its horizontal demand curve never touches minimum ATC.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Horizontal Tangency Error): A horizontal demand curve can ONLY be tangent to a U-shaped ATC curve at its exact minimum point, giving zero excess capacity.

questions.title: Graphical Impact of Brand Differentiation in the Short Run
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a local coffee roaster launches a distinctive single-origin cold-brew blend that strengthens customer loyalty in the short run (before rival cafés can copy it or new cafés enter). How does this change the roaster's short-run demand curve?

hints.text: Think about both total demand at every price and how sensitive loyal customers are to price changes.
Higher popularity shifts demand outward, while stronger brand loyalty makes demand less price-elastic (steeper).

options_template.text: Its demand curve shifts leftward and becomes completely horizontal.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Direction & Elasticity Inversion): Stronger customer appeal expands demand rightward and reduces price sensitivity rather than turning the firm into a price taker.

options_template.text: The roaster simply moves downward along its original demand curve without any shift.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Movement vs. Shift Error): A change in product quality or consumer tastes shifts the entire demand curve rather than moving along a fixed curve.

options_template.text: Its demand curve remains unchanged, while its MC curve shifts vertically down to zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Cost Conflation): Consumer preference shifts alter the firm's demand curve, not its marginal cost of roasting coffee.

options_template.text: Its demand curve shifts rightward and becomes steeper (more inelastic), allowing a higher short-run markup above MC.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Successful product differentiation attracts more buyers (rightward shift) and strengthens brand loyalty (steeper, less elastic demand), widening short-run markup and economic profit until entry responds.

questions.title: Ordering Outcomes Along the Oligopoly Spectrum
questions.prompt_template: On the oligopoly output-price spectrum graph with linear market demand D and constant marginal cost MC, how do industry output and market price compare across a cartel (Q_cartel, P_cartel), a non-cooperative oligopoly (Q_olig, P_olig), and a competitive benchmark (Q_C, P_C)?

hints.text: Locate the three dots along the downward-sloping market demand curve from top-left to bottom-right.
Remember that moving rightward along a downward-sloping demand curve raises Q and lowers P.

options_template.text: Q_cartel < Q_olig < Q_C and P_cartel > P_olig > P_C = MC.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Non-cooperative oligopoly settles strictly between the monopoly/cartel benchmark (lowest output, highest price) and the competitive benchmark (highest output, price equal to MC).

options_template.text: Q_cartel = Q_olig < Q_C and P_cartel = P_olig > P_C.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Perfect-Collusion Assumption): Non-cooperative oligopolists compete by expanding output past Q_cartel, pushing P_olig strictly below P_cartel.

options_template.text: Q_cartel > Q_olig > Q_C and P_cartel < P_olig < P_C.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Order Inversion): A cartel restricts output to the lowest level and charges the highest price, not the reverse.

options_template.text: Q_cartel < Q_C < Q_olig and P_cartel > P_C > P_olig.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Below-MC Pricing Error): Profit-maximizing oligopolists do not expand output past the competitive level where price would fall below marginal cost.

questions.topic: Cartel Breakdown on the Market Demand Graph
questions.title: Graphical Path When a Cartel Breaks Down
questions.prompt_template: Suppose an oligopoly cartel initially operates at (Q_cartel, P_cartel) on a linear market demand curve with constant MC. When members begin cheating on quotas and competing non-cooperatively, how is this transition represented on the market diagram?

hints.text: Ask whether cartel cheating changes consumer willingness to pay (shifting D) or changes industry quantity supplied along D.
Trace the path from (Q_cartel, P_cartel) to (Q_olig, P_olig) on the market demand curve.

options_template.text: A leftward shift of the entire market demand curve until it passes through the origin.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Movement vs. Shift Confusion): Cheating by producers changes industry output and price without shifting consumers' underlying market demand curve.

options_template.text: A movement downward and rightward along the fixed market demand curve from (Q_cartel, P_cartel) toward (Q_olig, P_olig) and (Q_C, P_C).
options_template.feedback: Correct. As cartel members expand output above quotas, total industry quantity rises and market price falls—represented as a southeast movement along the unchanged market demand curve.

options_template.text: A movement upward and leftward along the market demand curve toward higher prices and lower output.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Direction Inversion): Moving northwest along D represents tighter output restriction (stronger collusion), whereas cartel breakdown expands output and lowers price.

options_template.text: An upward shift of the constant marginal cost line until MC equals P_cartel.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Shift Confusion): Cartel cheating alters output discipline, not the firms' marginal production cost.

questions.title: Finding the Cartel Output and Price on a Linear Demand Graph
questions.prompt_template: On a market diagram with linear inverse demand D, industry marginal revenue MR (twice as steep as D), and horizontal constant MC, how is the joint profit-maximizing cartel point (Q_cartel, P_cartel) determined?

hints.text: A perfectly coordinated cartel acts like a single multi-plant monopolist.
First intersect industry MR with MC to find Q_cartel, then read price off the market demand curve.

options_template.text: Intersect D with MC to find Q_cartel, then move horizontally to MR to read P_cartel.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Competitive Intersection Error): Intersecting D with MC gives the competitive output Q_C, not the cartel output Q_cartel.

options_template.text: Intersect MR with MC to find both Q_cartel and P_cartel directly at that intersection point.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (MR-Curve Pricing Error): Reading price at the MR = MC intersection sets P = MC, giving away all cartel markup instead of pricing up on D.

options_template.text: Intersect MR with MC to find Q_cartel, then move vertically up to the market demand curve D to read P_cartel.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A profit-maximizing cartel sets industry MR = MC to choose Q_cartel and then charges the highest price consumers will pay for that quantity on the market demand curve D.

options_template.text: Choose the midpoint where MR crosses the horizontal axis regardless of the height of MC.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-MC Assumption): Setting MR = 0 maximizes revenue rather than profit whenever MC > 0.

questions.title: Reading Underlined Best Responses in a 2x2 Payoff Matrix
questions.prompt_template: When solving a 2x2 simultaneous payoff matrix using the underline (best-response) method, how do you visually identify a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium cell?

hints.text: Recall what each player's underlined payoff means within a column (for the Row player) or within a row (for the Column player).
A Nash equilibrium requires BOTH players to be playing best responses simultaneously.

options_template.text: It is any cell containing the single largest individual payoff anywhere in the matrix.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Temptation-Cell Fallacy): The largest single payoff often occurs in an asymmetric cheating cell where the other player is NOT playing a best response.

options_template.text: It is always the top-left cell where the sum of the two payoffs is maximized.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Joint-Maximum Fallacy): The highest-sum cell is the cooperative outcome, which often has neither payoff underlined in a Prisoner's Dilemma.

options_template.text: It is any cell where exactly one player's payoff is underlined and the other player's payoff is not.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (One-Sided Best-Response Error): If one player's payoff is not underlined, that player has a profitable unilateral deviation, so the cell is unstable.

options_template.text: It is any cell in which BOTH the Row player's payoff and the Column player's payoff are underlined.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When both payoffs in a cell are underlined, the Row player cannot improve by moving vertically within that column and the Column player cannot improve by moving horizontally within that row—the exact definition of Nash equilibrium.

questions.topic: Unilateral Deviation in the Streaming Pricing Matrix
questions.title: Why (Price High, Price High) Unravels in the 2x2 Pricing Matrix
questions.prompt_template: In the streaming-platform payoff matrix—(High, High) = ($50M, $50M), (High, Discount) = ($20M, $65M), (Discount, High) = ($65M, $20M), (Discount, Discount) = ($35M, $35M)—why is (High, High) NOT a Nash equilibrium?

hints.text: Hold one firm fixed at 'Price High' and compare the other firm's payoff from staying High versus switching to Discount.
Trace whether either firm has a profitable vertical or horizontal move out of the top-left cell.

options_template.text: Because starting from (High, High), either firm can unilaterally switch to Discount and raise its own profit from $50M to $65M.
options_template.feedback: Correct. At (High, High), Firm A gains +$15M by moving down to Discount ($65M > $50M), and Firm B gains +$15M by moving right to Discount ($65M > $50M); hence neither is playing a best response.

options_template.text: Because total industry profit ($100M) is lower at (High, High) than at (Discount, Discount) ($70M).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Arithmetic Inversion): Combined industry profit is higher at (High, High) ($100M > $70M); instability arises from individual unilateral gain, not low joint profit.

options_template.text: Because if one firm switches to Discount, its profit drops from $50M to $20M.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Row-Column Payoff Swap): $20M is the payoff of the rival who stays High while the other firm discounts; the firm that switches to Discount earns $65M.

options_template.text: Because (High, High) yields equal payoffs for both firms, and Nash equilibria must always be asymmetric.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Symmetry Misconception): Symmetric games frequently have symmetric Nash equilibria—indeed (Discount, Discount) = ($35M, $35M) is symmetric.

questions.title: Interpreting Cournot Duopoly Reaction Curves
questions.prompt_template: In a symmetric Cournot duopoly with linear demand and constant MC, Firm 1's best-response function is q_1*(q_2) = 45 - 0.5 q_2 and Firm 2's is q_2*(q_1) = 45 - 0.5 q_1. On a graph with q_1 on the horizontal axis and q_2 on the vertical axis, what do the downward slopes and intersection of these two curves signify?

hints.text: Examine what happens to q_1* when q_2 increases, and recall what holds simultaneously at the intersection of two best-response curves.
Downward-sloping reaction curves show how a firm adjusts its quantity when its rival produces more.

options_template.text: Downward slopes mean firms raise output whenever rivals raise output, and the intersection represents the joint profit-maximizing cartel output.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope & Cartel Confusion): A negative slope (-0.5) means q_1* falls when q_2 rises, and the intersection (30, 30) gives total output 60 > 45 (the cartel output).

options_template.text: Downward slopes show that each firm optimally contracts its own output when its rival produces more, and the intersection (30, 30) is the Cournot-Nash equilibrium where both firms play mutual best responses.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Higher rival output depresses residual demand and price, so each firm's best response is to produce less (negative slope); where the two curves cross at (30, 30), neither firm wishes to alter its output.

options_template.text: The vertical intercept (45) is the competitive industry output, and the intersection (30, 30) drives price down to marginal cost.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Intercept Conflation): When q_2 = 0, Firm 1 acts as a monopolist producing q_1 = 45 (the monopoly output, not competitive output 90), and at (30, 30) price ($40) still exceeds MC ($10).

options_template.text: Because both curves slope downward, they never intersect and no Nash equilibrium exists.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Geometric Intersection Error): Because the two lines have different slopes in (q_1, q_2) space (slope -2 vs. -0.5), they cross cleanly at the unique Cournot-Nash equilibrium (30, 30).

questions.title: Solving Long-Run Output and Price for an Artisan Bakery
questions.prompt_template: An artisan bakery in long-run monopolistic competition faces linear inverse demand P = 60 - 3q (with marginal revenue MR = 60 - 6q), constant marginal cost MC = $12 per loaf, and daily fixed overhead of $192 (so ATC = 192/q + 12). What are the bakery's long-run equilibrium output (q_LR) and price (P_LR)?

hints.text: Apply the profit-maximizing rule MR = MC to find q_LR first.
Substitute q_LR back into the inverse demand curve P = 60 - 3q, then verify that P_LR = ATC(q_LR).

options_template.text: q_LR = 16 loaves and P_LR = $12.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Perfect-Competition Rule): Setting P = MC (60 - 3q = 12) yields q = 16 and P = $12, ignoring that a differentiated firm sets MR = MC and would incur a loss at P = $12 < ATC.

options_template.text: q_LR = 8 loaves and P_LR = $12.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (MC-Pricing Error): Although q_LR = 8 is correct from MR = MC, price must be read from the demand curve P = 60 - 3(8) = $36, not set equal to MC = $12.

options_template.text: q_LR = 8 loaves and P_LR = $36.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Setting MR = MC gives 60 - 6q = 12, so 6q = 48 and q_LR = 8 loaves. Substituting into demand gives P_LR = 60 - 3(8) = $36, which exactly equals ATC(8) = 192/8 + 12 = $36 (zero economic profit).

options_template.text: q_LR = 12 loaves and P_LR = $24.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (MR-Slope Calculation Error): For linear inverse demand P = 60 - 3q, MR has double the slope (MR = 60 - 6q, not 60 - 4q); solving 60 - 4q = 12 incorrectly gives q = 12.

questions.title: Computing Short-Run Economic Profit for a Specialty Roaster
questions.prompt_template: A specialty coffee roaster faces short-run inverse demand P = 42 - 2q (with MR = 42 - 4q), constant marginal cost MC = $6 per bag, and daily fixed costs of $100. What is the roaster's maximum short-run economic profit?

hints.text: Find the profit-maximizing quantity q* from MR = MC and the price P* from the demand curve.
Compute Total Revenue (P* x q*) and subtract Total Cost (FC + MC x q*).

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed-Cost Omission): $162 = TR ($216) - VC ($54) omits the $100 daily fixed cost; subtracting FC leaves $62.
Diagnostic fallacy (Revenue-Profit Conflation): $216 = $24 x 9 is Total Revenue before deducting either variable cost ($54) or fixed cost ($100).

Diagnostic fallacy (Competitive Pricing Fallacy): Setting P = MC gives q = 18 and P = $6, leaving zero contribution margin to cover fixed costs and yielding a -$100 loss instead of maximizing profit at MR = MC.
Correct. Setting MR = MC gives 42 - 4q = 6, so q* = 9 bags and P* = 42 - 2(9) = $24. Thus TR = $24 x 9 = $216, TC = $100 + $6(9) = $154, and economic profit = $216 - $154 = $62.

questions.title: Measuring Excess Capacity from Linear Demand and U-Shaped ATC
questions.prompt_template: A monopolistically competitive hair salon in long-run equilibrium faces inverse demand P = 30 - 0.75q (with MR = 30 - 1.5q), marginal cost MC = 10 + 0.5q, and U-shaped ATC = 100/q + 10 + 0.25q, which reaches its minimum (efficient scale) at q_eff = 20 haircuts per day. What is the salon's excess capacity?

hints.text: First solve MR = MC to find the salon's long-run equilibrium output q_LR.
Excess capacity is the horizontal output difference (q_eff - q_LR).

options_template.text: 10 haircuts per day.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Setting MR = MC gives 30 - 1.5q = 10 + 0.5q, so 2q = 20 and q_LR = 10 (where P_LR = ATC = $22.50). Excess capacity is q_eff - q_LR = 20 - 10 = 10 haircuts per day.

options_template.text: 4 haircuts per day.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (P = MC Rule Error): Setting P = MC (30 - 0.75q = 10 + 0.5q) yields q = 16 and 20 - 16 = 4, forgetting that a differentiated firm maximizes profit at MR = MC.

options_template.text: 7.5 haircuts per day.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Markup-Excess Capacity Confusion): $7.50 = P_LR ($22.50) - MC_LR ($15.00) is the vertical dollar markup per haircut, not the horizontal output shortfall in haircuts.

options_template.text: 0 haircuts per day.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Perfect-Competition Carryover): Only perfectly competitive firms produce at q_eff with zero excess capacity in the long run.

questions.title: Finding Markup and Implied Fixed Cost in Long-Run Equilibrium
questions.prompt_template: A boutique yoga studio in long-run monopolistic competition earns zero economic profit while facing inverse demand P = 80 - 4q (with MR = 80 - 8q) and constant marginal cost MC = $16 per class. What are the studio's markup over marginal cost (P_LR - MC) and its implied daily fixed cost (FC)?

hints.text: Solve MR = MC for q_LR, then compute P_LR on the demand curve and markup = P_LR - MC.
Because economic profit is zero (TR = FC + MC x q_LR), implied FC equals (P_LR - MC) x q_LR.

options_template.text: Markup = $16 per class; FC = $128.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (MC-Markup Swap): $16 is the constant marginal cost itself (and $16 x 8 = $128 is total variable cost), not the markup (P_LR - MC).

options_template.text: Markup = $32 per class; FC = $256.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Setting MR = MC gives 80 - 8q = 16, so q_LR = 8 classes and P_LR = 80 - 4(8) = $48. Markup = $48 - $16 = $32 per class; for zero economic profit, FC = ($48 - $16) x 8 = $256.

options_template.text: Markup = $0 per class; FC = $0.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Profit Markup Fallacy): Zero economic profit means P_LR = ATC, not P_LR = MC; the positive markup covers the studio's fixed overhead.

options_template.text: Markup = $48 per class; FC = $384.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Markup Conflation): $48 is the full class price P_LR and $384 = $48 x 8 is Total Revenue; subtracting MC ($16) gives a $32 markup and $256 FC.

questions.title: Calculating CR4 and HHI in a Six-Firm Cloud Market
questions.prompt_template: A regional cloud-storage market is served by six firms with market shares of 35%, 25%, 15%, 10%, 10%, and 5%. What are the Four-Firm Concentration Ratio (CR4) and the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI)?

hints.text: CR4 sums only the four largest firms' market shares, while HHI sums the squared shares of ALL six firms.

options_template.text: CR4 = 85% and HHI = 2,175.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Truncated-HHI Error): 2,175 = 35^2 + 25^2 + 15^2 + 10^2 omits the fifth (10^2 = 100) and sixth (5^2 = 25) firms; HHI must sum squared shares across all firms.
Diagnostic fallacy (All-Firm CR4 Error): Summing all six shares always gives 100%; CR4 includes only the four largest firms (85%).

options_template.text: CR4 = 85% and HHI = 2,300.
CR4 = 85% and HHI = 7,225.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sum-Then-Square Fallacy): 7,225 = 85^2 squares the summed top-four share instead of summing each individual firm's squared share.

questions.title: Evaluating a Horizontal Merger via Post-Merger HHI and Delta HHI
questions.prompt_template: Five broadband providers serve a regional market with shares of 30%, 25%, 20%, 15%, and 10% (baseline HHI = 2,250). If the 20% provider and the 15% provider merge into a single 35% firm (assuming no customer defection), what are the post-merger HHI and the change in HHI (Delta HHI)?

hints.text: Write down the new four-firm shares (35%, 30%, 25%, 10%) and square each one.
Cross-check your change using the algebraic shortcut Delta HHI = 2 x s_A x s_B.

options_template.text: Post-merger HHI = 2,550 and Delta HHI = +300.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Missing Factor-of-2 Error): Expanding (s_A + s_B)^2 - (s_A^2 + s_B^2) yields 2*s_A*s_B = 2(20)(15) = +600, not s_A*s_B = +300.

options_template.text: Post-merger HHI = 3,475 and Delta HHI = +1,225.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Double-Counting Pre-Merger Shares): Adding 35^2 = 1,225 directly to 2,250 fails to subtract the eliminated pre-merger squares (20^2 + 15^2 = 625).

options_template.text: Post-merger HHI = 2,250 and Delta HHI = 0.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Constant-Sum Fallacy): Although total shares still sum to 100%, squaring combined shares always increases HHI when two positive-share firms merge.

options_template.text: Post-merger HHI = 2,850 and Delta HHI = +600.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Post-merger shares (35%, 30%, 25%, 10%) yield HHI_post = 1,225 + 900 + 625 + 100 = 2,850, so Delta HHI = 2,850 - 2,250 = +600 (matching 2 x 20 x 15 = 600).

questions.title: Computing Cartel and Competitive Benchmarks on Linear Demand
questions.prompt_template: An oligopoly industry faces linear market inverse demand P = 140 - 2Q (with industry MR = 140 - 4Q) and constant marginal cost MC = $20 per unit. What are the joint profit-maximizing cartel output and price (Q_cartel, P_cartel), and what is the competitive benchmark output (Q_C)?

hints.text: For the cartel outcome, set industry MR = MC to find Q_cartel, then plug Q_cartel into P = 140 - 2Q.
For the competitive benchmark, set P = MC (140 - 2Q = 20) to solve for Q_C.

options_template.text: Q_cartel = 30, P_cartel = $80, and Q_C = 60.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Cartel: MR = MC gives 140 - 4Q = 20, so Q_cartel = 30 and P_cartel = 140 - 2(30) = $80. Competitive benchmark: P = MC gives 140 - 2Q = 20, so Q_C = 60.

options_template.text: Q_cartel = 60, P_cartel = $20, and Q_C = 30.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Benchmark Reversal): A cartel restricts output below the competitive level (30 < 60) and charges a price above MC ($80 > $20).

options_template.text: Q_cartel = 30, P_cartel = $20, and Q_C = 60.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (MC-Pricing Error): At Q_cartel = 30, consumers are willing to pay P = 140 - 2(30) = $80 on the demand curve, not $20.

options_template.text: Q_cartel = 35, P_cartel = $70, and Q_C = 70.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-MC Omission): Setting MR = 0 (Q = 35) and P = 0 (Q = 70) ignores the constant marginal cost of $20 per unit.

questions.title: Quantifying the Unilateral Incentive to Cheat on a Cartel Quota
questions.prompt_template: Two identical firms form a cartel facing market inverse demand P = 120 - Q and constant MC = $20. They maximize joint profit at Q = 50 (each producing its quota of 25 units at P = $70, earning $1,250 each). If Firm 1 secretly cheats by raising its output to 35 units while Firm 2 sticks to 25 units, what is Firm 1's new profit and net gain from cheating?

hints.text: First find the new total industry output Q = q_1 + q_2 and the new market price P = 120 - Q.
Compute Firm 1's cheating profit as (P - MC) x q_1, then subtract its cartel profit of $1,250.

options_template.text: $1,750 (a net gain of +$500).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed-Price Cheating Error): Multiplying ($70 - $20) x 35 = $1,750 ignores that adding 10 extra units pushes total output to Q = 60 and drops market price from $70 to $60.

options_template.text: $1,400 (a net gain of +$150).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Total output rises to Q = 35 + 25 = 60, lowering price to P = 120 - 60 = $60. Firm 1 earns ($60 - $20) x 35 = $1,400, gaining $1,400 - $1,250 = +$150 by cheating.

options_template.text: $1,000 (a net loss of -$250).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Compliant-Firm Substitution): ($60 - $20) x 25 = $1,000 is the reduced profit suffered by Firm 2 (the compliant partner), not Firm 1 (the cheater).

options_template.text: $2,100 (a net gain of +$850).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Revenue-Profit Conflation): $60 x 35 = $2,100 is Firm 1's total revenue before subtracting its variable cost ($20 x 35 = $700).

questions.title: Nash Equilibrium and Foregone Profit in an Advertising Game
questions.prompt_template: Two rival beverage firms, FizzCo and PopCo, simultaneously choose 'Low Ads' or 'High Ads'. Annual profits (FizzCo, PopCo) are: (Low Ads, Low Ads) = ($40M, $40M); (Low Ads, High Ads) = ($15M, $55M); (High Ads, Low Ads) = ($55M, $15M); (High Ads, High Ads) = ($25M, $25M). What is the unique Nash equilibrium, and how much combined industry profit is foregone compared to mutual 'Low Ads'?

hints.text: Check each firm's best response when the rival plays Low Ads, and again when the rival plays High Ads.
Sum both firms' profits at (Low Ads, Low Ads) and subtract their combined profits at the Nash equilibrium.

options_template.text: (Low Ads, Low Ads) with payoffs ($40M, $40M), foregoing $0M in combined profit.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cooperative-Outcome Error): Although (Low Ads, Low Ads) maximizes joint profit ($80M), each firm can unilaterally switch to High Ads to raise its own profit from $40M to $55M.

options_template.text: (High Ads, High Ads) with payoffs ($25M, $25M), foregoing $15M in combined profit.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Single-Firm Loss Reporting): Each individual firm loses $15M ($40M - $25M), so combined industry profit foregone across both firms is $15M + $15M = $30M.

options_template.text: (High Ads, High Ads) with payoffs ($25M, $25M), foregoing $30M in combined profit.
options_template.feedback: Correct. High Ads is strictly dominant for both firms ($55M > $40M and $25M > $15M), making (High Ads, High Ads) the unique Nash equilibrium. Combined profit drops from $80M to $50M, foregoing $30M.

options_template.text: (High Ads, Low Ads) with payoffs ($55M, $15M), foregoing $10M in combined profit.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Asymmetric Cell Error): At (High Ads, Low Ads), PopCo earns $15M and will profitably deviate to High Ads to earn $25M.

questions.title: Finding Nash Equilibrium When Only One Player Has a Dominant Strategy
questions.prompt_template: Two regional airlines, WestAir (Row) and BayJet (Column), simultaneously choose 'Hold Fare' or 'Match Fare'. Payoffs in millions (WestAir, BayJet) are: (Hold, Hold) = ($30M, $28M); (Hold, Match) = ($18M, $32M); (Match, Hold) = ($36M, $20M); (Match, Match) = ($24M, $16M). What is the pure-strategy Nash equilibrium?

hints.text: Check first whether WestAir has a dominant strategy across both columns, then find BayJet's best response to that choice.
Remember that a Nash equilibrium does NOT require both players to have dominant strategies.

options_template.text: (Hold, Hold) with payoffs ($30M, $28M).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Joint-Profit Maximization Error): (Hold, Hold) yields the highest combined profit ($58M), but both WestAir ($36M > $30M) and BayJet ($32M > $28M) have unilateral incentives to deviate.

options_template.text: (Match, Match) with payoffs ($24M, $16M).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Bottom-Right Habit Error): Not every 2x2 game has a bottom-right Nash equilibrium; at (Match, Match), BayJet improves its profit from $16M to $20M by switching to Hold.

options_template.text: No pure-strategy Nash equilibrium exists because BayJet has no dominant strategy.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Dominance-Required Fallacy): BayJet's lack of a dominant strategy does not prevent a Nash equilibrium; once WestAir plays its dominant strategy (Match), BayJet has a clear best response (Hold).

options_template.text: (Match, Hold) with payoffs ($36M, $20M).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Match is strictly dominant for WestAir ($36M > $30M and $24M > $18M). Given WestAir plays Match, BayJet's best response is Hold ($20M > $16M), making (Match, Hold) the unique Nash equilibrium.

questions.title: Solving Symmetric Cournot Best-Response Functions
questions.prompt_template: Two symmetric quantity-setting (Cournot) duopolists face linear market inverse demand P = 130 - (q_1 + q_2) and constant marginal cost MC = $10. Their continuous best-response functions are q_1*(q_2) = 60 - 0.5 q_2 and q_2*(q_1) = 60 - 0.5 q_1. What are each firm's Cournot-Nash equilibrium output (q*) and the resulting market price (P*)?

hints.text: Use symmetry (q_1* = q_2* = q*) to substitute q* into q* = 60 - 0.5 q*.
Remember that market price depends on TOTAL industry output Q* = q_1* + q_2*.

options_template.text: q_1* = q_2* = 40 units and P* = $50.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Setting q* = 60 - 0.5q* gives 1.5q* = 60, so q_1* = q_2* = 40 units. Total industry output is Q* = 80, yielding market price P* = 130 - 80 = $50.

options_template.text: q_1* = q_2* = 30 units and P* = $70.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cartel-Split Substitution): Q = 60 (30 per firm) at P = $70 is the collusive monopoly outcome, not the non-cooperative Cournot-Nash equilibrium.

options_template.text: q_1* = q_2* = 60 units and P* = $10.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Rival / Competitive Error): Setting q_2 = 0 gives q_1 = 60; if both produce 60, Q = 120 drives P down to MC = $10, which is not a best response to q_2 = 60.

options_template.text: q_1* = q_2* = 40 units and P* = $90.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Single-Firm Output Substitution): Plugging only one firm's output (40) into P = 130 - Q gives $90; total market output is q_1 + q_2 = 80, giving P* = $50.

questions.title: Computing Per-Firm Profit in a Cournot-Nash Equilibrium
questions.prompt_template: Two symmetric Cournot duopolists face market inverse demand P = 160 - 2(q_1 + q_2) and constant marginal cost MC = $40 (with zero fixed cost). Each firm's best-response function is q_i*(q_j) = 30 - 0.5 q_j. What is each firm's profit in the symmetric Cournot-Nash equilibrium?

hints.text: Solve q* = 30 - 0.5 q* for each firm's output, then compute total output Q* = 2q* and market price P* = 160 - 2Q*.
Calculate per-firm profit as (P* - MC) x q*.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Total Revenue or Combined-Profit Confusion): $1,600 is either one firm's Total Revenue ($80 x 20, ignoring MC = $40) or the COMBINED profit of both firms ($800 + $800).
Correct. Solving q* = 30 - 0.5q* gives q_1* = q_2* = 20 units, so Q* = 40 and P* = 160 - 2(40) = $80. Each firm earns profit = ($80 - $40) x 20 = $800.
Diagnostic fallacy (Mixed Price-Quantity Error): Combining the collusive cartel price ($100) with Cournot output (20) yields ($100 - $40) x 20 = $1,200, violating the market demand curve at Q = 40.

Diagnostic fallacy (Cartel-Profit Substitution): $900 = ($100 - $40) x 15 is each firm's profit under perfect cartel collusion (Q = 30), whereas non-cooperative Cournot competition lowers per-firm profit to $800.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Evaluating Regulatory Proposals to Eliminate Excess Capacity
questions.prompt_template: A municipal planner observes that neighborhood cafés operate with excess capacity during afternoon hours and proposes forcing all cafés to standardize their menus and merge into fewer large cafeterias so each operates at minimum ATC. Why do most economists caution against this policy?

hints.text: Review the 'Clear It Up' box on whether excess capacity in monopolistic competition is pure social waste.
Compare the modest average-cost savings against what consumers lose when product variety and neighborhood convenience disappear.

options_template.text: Because monopolistically competitive firms already achieve both allocative efficiency (P = MC) and productive efficiency (q = q_eff).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Efficiency Misstatement): Monopolistic competition exhibits neither P = MC nor q = q_eff; economists accept this trade-off because variety itself has positive value to consumers.

options_template.text: Because forcing firms to produce at minimum ATC would automatically double their economic profits.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Profit Conflation): Lowering average cost under competitive entry passes savings to consumers rather than guaranteeing permanently higher economic profits.

options_template.text: Because eliminating product differentiation and neighborhood convenience could reduce consumer welfare by more than the small average-cost reduction gained from removing excess capacity.
options_template.feedback: Correct. In monopolistic competition, excess capacity and a modest markup represent the economic trade-off society willingly pays for product diversity, tailored ambiance, and local convenience.

options_template.text: Because merging cafés into fewer large outlets would make each remaining outlet's demand curve perfectly horizontal.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Concentration-Elasticity Inversion): Reducing the number of competing cafés increases market concentration rather than creating perfect competition.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Entry Restrictions in Differentiated Retail Markets
questions.title: Economic Impact of Capping New Café Permits
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a city enacts a strict zoning cap prohibiting any new coffee shops from opening in a rapidly growing neighborhood where existing cafés currently earn positive economic profits. What is the most likely long-run market outcome?

hints.text: Ask which adjustment mechanism normally drives long-run economic profits to zero in monopolistic competition.
Trace what happens when that mechanism is blocked by a legal entry barrier.

options_template.text: Existing cafés will voluntarily lower prices to MC so that their economic profits fall to zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Voluntary-Competitive Fallacy): Without new entrants shifting incumbent demand curves inward, profit-maximizing cafés have no incentive to cut prices to MC.

options_template.text: The neighborhood coffee market will transition into perfect competition with horizontal firm demand.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Barrier-Competition Inversion): Adding entry barriers moves a market away from competition toward oligopoly or monopoly power, never toward perfect competition.

options_template.text: Incumbent cafés will immediately suffer economic losses because fixed costs vanish when entry is blocked.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Entry-Loss Inversion): Blocking new competitors protects incumbents' customer base rather than causing losses, and zoning caps do not eliminate fixed costs.

options_template.text: The legal barrier to entry prevents incumbent demand curves from shifting inward, allowing existing cafés to retain positive economic profits while limiting consumer variety.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Free entry is the force that erodes short-run economic profits in monopolistic competition; capping permits shields incumbents from competition, preserving economic rents and reducing variety.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Long-Run Survival Under Zero Economic Profit
questions.title: Why Owners Stay Open Despite Zero Long-Run Economic Profit
questions.prompt_template: After several competing studios open nearby, the owner of an independent yoga studio realizes she is now earning zero economic profit in long-run equilibrium. A friend advises her to shut down immediately because 'working for zero profit makes no sense.' How should an economist evaluate this advice?

hints.text: Remember what costs are included inside Average Total Cost (ATC) in microeconomics.
Compare the owner's total compensation inside the studio against her next-best alternative outside the studio.

options_template.text: The friend is wrong because zero economic profit means the owner is earning a normal profit that fully matches her next-best alternative use of time and capital, so exiting would not leave her better off.
options_template.feedback: Correct. At P = ATC, the studio covers every explicit bill and pays the owner a competitive return equal to her opportunity cost; leaving the industry would yield no higher economic payoff.

options_template.text: The friend is right because zero economic profit means the owner takes home $0 in personal income.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Income Myth): Zero economic profit includes a normal profit compensating the owner for the full opportunity cost of her labor and invested capital.

options_template.text: The friend is right because zero economic profit guarantees the studio will soon incur negative accounting profit.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Equilibrium-Instability Error): Zero economic profit is a stable long-run equilibrium with positive accounting profit—neither entry nor exit is triggered.

options_template.text: The friend is wrong because monopolistically competitive firms can simply raise price above their demand curve whenever profits fall.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Off-Demand Pricing Fallacy): A firm can only choose price-quantity pairs on or below its demand curve; charging above demand leaves unsold capacity and lowers profit.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why Coffee Shops Proliferate While Wireless Carriers Stay Concentrated
questions.prompt_template: Reflecting on the chapter's 'Bring It Home' question, why do college neighborhoods support dozens of competing independent coffee shops while nationwide wireless cellular service remains concentrated among only a few major carriers?

hints.text: Compare the capital requirements, economies of scale, and regulatory/resource barriers required to enter each industry.
Match each industry to its corresponding market structure (monopolistic competition vs. oligopoly).

options_template.text: Coffee drinkers have identical tastes, whereas wireless customers demand completely unique custom-built cell towers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Differentiation Inversion): Coffee shops thrive on product differentiation, whereas wireless concentration is driven by massive scale economies and scarce spectrum licenses.

options_template.text: Opening a café requires modest startup capital and faces low entry barriers, whereas building a nationwide cellular network involves massive economies of scale and scarce spectrum licenses that create formidable barriers to entry.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Low entry barriers keep cafés monopolistically competitive, while huge fixed infrastructure costs (economies of scale) and scarce radio spectrum licenses keep national wireless service an oligopoly.

options_template.text: Antitrust law forbids more than four wireless carriers from operating, while subsidizing every neighborhood café.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Regulatory Fabrication): Wireless oligopoly stems primarily from structural scale economies and spectrum scarcity, not a statutory four-firm cap.

options_template.text: Wireless carriers face zero marginal cost and therefore must be perfectly competitive.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Low-MC Competition Fallacy): High fixed costs coupled with low marginal cost actually generate strong economies of scale that favor concentrated oligopolies or natural monopolies, not perfect competition.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Antitrust Policy: Why Regulators Prefer HHI Over CR4
questions.title: Evaluating a Merger Inside a Four-Firm Oligopoly
questions.prompt_template: In a regional wireless market served by four providers with market shares of 40%, 30%, 20%, and 10%, the two smallest firms propose to merge. Their attorneys argue the merger is harmless because the Four-Firm Concentration Ratio (CR4) does not change at all. How would DOJ/FTC antitrust economists counter this argument?

hints.text: Check what happens to CR4 versus HHI when a 4-firm market consolidates into a 3-firm market.
Remember that HHI rises by 2 x s_A x s_B = 2(20)(10) = +400 points.

options_template.text: CR4 falls from 100% to 70% after the merger, proving that market power decreased.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Firm-Count Misinterpretation): After merging into three firms (40%, 30%, 30%), the top four (in fact top three) still hold 100% of the market.

options_template.text: The merger actually increases CR4 from 100% to 130%, which violates statutory limits.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Percentage-Bound Error): Market shares always sum to 100%, so CR4 can never exceed 100%.

options_template.text: CR4 is blind to consolidation among the top four firms (staying fixed at 100%), whereas the HHI captures the loss of a rival and rises sharply by +400 points (from 3,000 to 3,400).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because CR4 merely sums the top four shares, it stays stuck at 100% even as a four-firm market shrinks to three firms; HHI properly flags the +400-point jump in concentration.

options_template.text: The attorneys are right because HHI also remains unchanged whenever total market share stays at 100%.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Squared-Share Oversight): Squaring combined shares adds 2*s_A*s_B = +400 to HHI even though total shares still sum to 100%.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Comparing Horizontal Mergers of Small vs. Large Rivals
questions.prompt_template: Consider two proposed horizontal mergers in separate regional markets that each currently have an HHI of 2,000: Merger X combines two small firms with 5% and 4% market shares, whereas Merger Y combines two leading firms with 30% and 20% market shares. Why do antitrust authorities scrutinize Merger Y far more intensely than Merger X?

hints.text: Use the merger change formula Delta HHI = 2 x s_A x s_B to compare the concentration impact of both mergers.
Contrast Delta HHI = +40 against Delta HHI = +1,200 in terms of lost competitive constraint.

options_template.text: Because Merger Y reduces HHI by 1,200 points, threatening destructive below-cost pricing.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Error): Merging two horizontal competitors always increases HHI (never decreases it) because (s_A + s_B)^2 > s_A^2 + s_B^2.

options_template.text: Because Merger X increases HHI by more points than Merger Y whenever baseline HHI is 2,000.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Magnitude Inversion): 2(5)(4) = +40 is 30 times smaller than 2(30)(20) = +1,200; baseline HHI does not reverse this comparison.

options_template.text: Because antitrust agencies automatically block any merger involving a firm with less than 10% market share.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Policy Inversion): Small fringe mergers generate tiny HHI changes and rarely threaten competition, whereas large incumbent mergers trigger strict scrutiny.

options_template.text: Because Merger Y raises HHI by +1,200 points (2 x 30 x 20), creating a dominant 50% firm and sharply increasing market power, whereas Merger X raises HHI by only +40 points (2 x 5 x 4).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because Delta HHI = 2*s_A*s_B scales multiplicatively with merging firms' shares, consolidating two large rivals drastically raises market concentration and unilateral pricing power compared to merging two tiny fringe firms.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Cartel Quota Enforcement in Global Oil Markets
questions.title: Why Wide Price-Cost Gaps Destabilize OPEC-Style Quotas
questions.prompt_template: In the chapter's illustrative OPEC quota example, suppose a cartel agreement holds crude oil at $90 per barrel while a member country's marginal extraction cost is $20 per barrel. Why does this wide $70 price-cost margin simultaneously make the cartel lucrative AND fragile?

hints.text: Consider both the collective reward of keeping the price at $90 and the private temptation to quietly pump extra barrels.
Trace what happens if multiple member countries act on that same temptation simultaneously.

options_template.text: A high price-cost gap creates high joint profits if everyone complies, yet it gives each member a large immediate gain ($70/barrel) from quietly pumping above quota—which, if imitated by rivals, floods supply and erodes the $90 price.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The exact same wedge (P - MC = $70) that makes collusion profitable also intensifies each member's unilateral incentive to cheat on its quota; widespread cheating pushes market supply out and depresses prices.

options_template.text: A wide price-cost margin eliminates any incentive to cheat because members prefer keeping oil underground rather than earning $70 per extra barrel.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cheating-Incentive Inversion): A larger (P - MC) margin strengthens—not eliminates—the short-run payoff from secretly exceeding a production quota.

options_template.text: Because marginal cost is $20, the cartel can legally enforce quotas in domestic antitrust courts.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Legal-Enforcement Fallacy): International cartels like OPEC lack a binding global court that can penalize sovereign members for exceeding quotas.

options_template.text: A $70 margin causes global oil demand to shift outward automatically, eliminating the need for quotas.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply-Demand Conflation): A cartel's price-cost margin does not shift global demand outward; holding price at $90 requires strict output restraint.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Welfare Implications When an Oligopoly Fails to Collude
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a three-firm oligopoly with constant marginal cost attempts to form a cartel, fails to sustain collusion, and settles into a non-cooperative oligopoly equilibrium. How do consumer surplus, industry output, and deadweight loss compare to the cartel outcome?
