hints.text: Use the oligopoly output-price spectrum (Q_cartel < Q_olig < Q_C and P_cartel > P_olig > P_C = MC).
Remember that moving closer to P = MC expands consumer surplus and shrinks deadweight loss, though deadweight loss does not reach zero until P = MC.

options_template.text: Industry output falls and deadweight loss expands because firms waste resources competing.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Competition-Welfare Inversion): Moving from a cartel to non-cooperative oligopoly increases output and lowers price, unambiguously reducing deadweight loss.

options_template.text: Industry output rises, price falls, consumer surplus increases, and deadweight loss shrinks relative to the cartel—though some deadweight loss remains because P_olig > MC.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Non-cooperative rivalry expands output past Q_cartel and lowers price below P_cartel, improving consumer surplus and reducing deadweight loss, yet leaving P_olig > MC so allocative efficiency is still incomplete.

options_template.text: Deadweight loss falls all the way to zero because any breakdown of a cartel immediately forces P = MC.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Immediate-Competition Fallacy): In quantity-setting or differentiated oligopoly, non-cooperative price P_olig remains strictly above MC, leaving residual deadweight loss.

options_template.text: Consumer surplus stays unchanged because total market demand did not shift.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Fixed-CS Fallacy): Even with an unchanged demand curve, a lower market price expands consumer surplus along the demand curve.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Antitrust Policy & the Pricing Prisoner's Dilemma
questions.title: Why Antitrust Laws Preserve Firms' Pricing Prisoner's Dilemma
questions.prompt_template: In a pricing Prisoner's Dilemma between two streaming platforms, both firms would earn higher profits if they could legally sign a binding agreement to hold prices high. Why do antitrust statutes strictly prohibit such explicit price-fixing agreements?

hints.text: Recall the 'Clear It Up' insight: who wins and who loses when competing firms are trapped in a low-price Nash equilibrium?
Compare the firms' joint-profit interest against society's broader consumer-welfare and allocative-efficiency interest.

options_template.text: Because binding price-fixing contracts violate the definition of product differentiation.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Irrelevant Mechanism): Antitrust prohibitions target anticompetitive collusion and consumer harm regardless of whether products are identical or differentiated.

options_template.text: Because price-fixing agreements force firms to set prices below marginal cost, driving them bankrupt.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price-Direction Inversion): Horizontal price-fixing agreements aim to hold prices artificially HIGH above marginal cost, not below marginal cost.

options_template.text: Because allowing firms to escape their pricing Prisoner's Dilemma via price-fixing transfers surplus from consumers to firms and creates deadweight loss through artificially restricted output.
options_template.feedback: Correct. While the non-cooperative Nash equilibrium hurts the two firms' combined profits, it benefits consumers via lower prices and higher output; antitrust law blocks collusion to protect consumer surplus and efficiency.

options_template.text: Because consumers earn higher surplus when firms successfully coordinate on the collusive (High, High) outcome.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Surplus Inversion): Higher collusive prices strictly reduce consumer surplus and raise firm profits.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: How Repeated Interaction Stabilizes Airline Fares Without Explicit Collusion
questions.prompt_template: Two major airlines compete daily on the San Francisco–Los Angeles nonstop route using automated pricing software that detects and matches any fare cut within hours. Why can this repeated interaction sustain higher average fares than a one-shot pricing Prisoner's Dilemma even without an explicit illegal meeting?

hints.text: Compare the payoff of undercutting a rival ONCE when the game ends immediately versus when the rival can retaliate on every future day.
Connect automated fare matching to the 'tit-for-tat' enforcement mechanism discussed in Section 9.3.

options_template.text: Because automated software legally converts the route into a regulated government monopoly.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Regulatory Confusion): Automated pricing is a private competitive tool, not a government monopoly franchise.

options_template.text: Because passengers stop comparing fares whenever airlines interact repeatedly.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand-Inattention Fallacy): Online travel platforms make fare comparison easy; fare stability arises from rivals' retaliatory incentives, not consumer blindness.

options_template.text: Because repeating a game changes every firm's marginal cost of jet fuel to zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Invariance Error): Repeated interaction changes strategic incentives over time, not physical operating costs.

options_template.text: Because in a repeated game, the credible threat of immediate tit-for-tat fare retaliation shrinks the short-term gain from undercutting and makes ongoing mutual restraint more profitable than triggering a prolonged fare war.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Repeated daily interaction allows tit-for-tat matching to punish defectors rapidly; when the discounted cost of future price wars outweighs a brief gain from undercutting, tacit fare stability can emerge.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Evaluating Price-Matching Guarantees in Oligopoly
questions.prompt_template: Two competing electronics chains advertise 'We will match any lower advertised price from a competitor!' Consumers often assume this guarantee guarantees fierce price cutting. Using game-theoretic reasoning, why might economists view price-matching guarantees skeptically as a potential facilitator of higher prices?

hints.text: Ask what happens to Firm B's gain from undercutting Firm A if Firm A is pre-committed to match Firm B's lower price automatically.
If undercutting no longer lets you steal your rival's customers at a lower price, does your incentive to cut price rise or fall?

options_template.text: By committing to match any rival's discount immediately, the guarantee eliminates a rival's temptation payoff from secretly undercutting, removing the incentive to launch price cuts in the first place.
options_template.feedback: Correct. In a pricing Prisoner's Dilemma, discounting is tempting only because it steals customers from a high-priced rival; automatic price-matching eliminates that temptation payoff and can help sustain high prices.

options_template.text: Because price-matching guarantees legally forbid either retailer from ever raising prices.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ceiling Confusion): A price-matching guarantee promises only to match a lower rival price, not to cap prices when both firms keep prices elevated.

options_template.text: Because matching a rival's price forces both retailers to operate at minimum ATC.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Scale Conflation): Price-matching alters strategic pricing payoffs rather than forcing firms to produce at efficient scale.

options_template.text: Because consumers refuse to buy from any store that advertises a price-matching policy.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Consumer-Boycott Assumption): Consumers generally welcome price-matching promises; the anti-competitive concern lies in how the commitment changes rivals' strategic incentives.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Game Theory Policy Synthesis: Advertising Arms Races
questions.title: Why Restricting a Costly Advertising Channel Can Paradoxically Raise Duopoly Profits
questions.prompt_template: Suppose two dominant soda companies are trapped in an advertising Prisoner's Dilemma: each spends heavily on national television commercials simply to defend market share from the other, leaving total industry sales nearly unchanged while both firms' profits drop. If public-health regulators ban national TV commercials for sugary sodas, what paradoxical effect could occur to the two firms' profits?

hints.text: Locate the pre-ban Nash equilibrium (High Ads, High Ads) and compare it to the regulated outcome (Low Ads, Low Ads) in an advertising Prisoner's Dilemma.
Notice how an external ban removes the dominant-strategy arms race that neither firm could stop unilaterally.

options_template.text: Both firms' profits must fall to zero because firms can never sell products without television ads.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Sales Fallacy): When rival ads largely cancel out in a mature duopoly, eliminating that mutually offsetting cost does not drive consumer demand to zero.

options_template.text: Both firms' profits could actually increase because the ban externally enforces the cooperative (Low Ads, Low Ads) outcome, saving both firms massive offsetting advertising costs.
options_template.feedback: Correct. In a symmetric advertising Prisoner's Dilemma, an industry-wide ban on a mutually canceling ad channel resolves the firms' commitment problem—moving them from (High Ads, High Ads) to higher-profit (Low Ads, Low Ads).

options_template.text: One firm will legally gain a pure monopoly while the other is forced out of business immediately.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Symmetric-Ban Asymmetry Error): An industry-wide ban applies equally to both dominant rivals rather than granting one firm a monopoly.

options_template.text: The ban turns the duopoly into a perfectly competitive market with P = MC.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Market-Structure Jump): Restricting one advertising channel does not remove entry barriers or turn a two-firm oligopoly into perfect competition.
